title: Γεωργὸς καὶ κύνες
part: The Farmer and the Dogs (Chambry 80 · Perry 52)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 80 (= Perry 52). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γεωργὸς ὑπὸ χειμῶνος ἐναποληφθεὶς ἐν τῇ ἐπαύλει, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἠδύνατο προελθεῖν καὶ ἑαυτῷ τροφὴν πορίσαι, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον τὰ πρόβατα κατέφαγεν.
sentences.tr: Geōrgos hypo cheimōnos enapolēphtheis en tēi epaulei, epeidē ouk ēdynato proelthein kai heautōi trophēn porisai, to men prōton ta probata katephagen.
sentences.l: A farmer, shut in by the winter storm in his farmstead, since he could not go out and procure food for himself, first of all ate the sheep.
sentences.n: ἐναποληφθείς is the aorist passive of ἐναπολαμβάνω, 'be caught and held inside'. χειμών is winter and storm at once — the season and the weather it brings. τὸ μὲν πρῶτον opens a count that the next two sentences finish.

sentences.t: Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἔτι ὁ χειμὼν ἐπέμενε, καὶ τὰς αἶγας κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Epeidē de eti ho cheimōn epemene, kai tas aigas katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And when the winter still held on, he made a banquet of the goats as well.
sentences.n: κατεθοινήσατο is built on θοίνη, a feast: a heavier word than the κατέφαγεν of the sheep, and the escalation is deliberate. καί here is 'also', not 'and'.

sentences.t: Ἐκ τρίτου δέ, ὡς οὐδεμία ἄνεσις ἐγίνετο, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀροτῆρας βοῦς ἐχώρησεν.
sentences.tr: Ek tritou de, hōs oudemia anesis egineto, kai epi tous arotēras bous echōrēsen.
sentences.l: And for the third time, as no relief came, he advanced against the ploughing oxen as well.
sentences.n: ἐκ τρίτου, 'for the third time'. ἄνεσις is a slackening of anything held tight — of weather here, of a rope elsewhere. χωρέω ἐπί with the accusative is the verb of an advance against an enemy, and the fable uses it of a man against his own beasts.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ κύνες θεασάμενοι τὰ πραττόμενα ἔφασαν πρὸς ἀλλήλους· « Ἀπιτέον ἡμῖν ἐνθένδε· ὁ δεσπότης γάρ, εἰ οὐδὲ τῶν συνεργαζομένων βοῶν ἀπέσχετο, ἡμῶν πῶς φείσεται ; »
sentences.tr: Hoi de kynes theasamenoi ta prattomena ephasan pros allēlous· « Apiteon hēmin enthende· ho despotēs gar, ei oude tōn synergazomenōn boōn apescheto, hēmōn pōs pheisetai ; »
sentences.l: And the dogs, having watched what was being done, said to one another: « We must go from here; for if the master did not hold off even from the oxen that work alongside him, how will he spare us? »
sentences.i: The dogs, seeing what was going on, said to one another: « We must leave this place; for if the master did not keep his hands off even the oxen that share his work, how will he spare us? »
sentences.n: ἀπιτέον is a verbal adjective in -τέον from ἄπειμι, 'go away', with ἡμῖν in the dative naming who must — Greek's ordinary way of saying 'we have to go'. ἀπέχομαι takes the genitive of what one holds off from. Chambry prints a space before his Greek question mark, as French typography does.

sentences.t: Ὁ λογός δηλοῖ ὅτι δεῖ τούτους μάλιστα φυλάττεσθαι οἳ οὐδὲ τῆς κατὰ τῶν οἰκείων ἀδικίας ἀπέχονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti dei toutous malista phylattesthai hoi oude tēs kata tōn oikeiōn adikias apechontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that one must guard above all against those who do not hold off even from injustice against their own.
sentences.n: Chambry prints Ὁ λογός here, with the accent on the last syllable where the word is ὁ λόγος; the transcription keeps his page as it stands rather than tidying it. οἱ οἰκεῖοι are one's own people, the household — which is exactly what the dogs are, and why they leave.
